papers.title_in_file: QuProFS: An Evolutionary Training-free Approach to Efficient Quantum Feature Map Search

figures.shows: The five-step QuProFS pipeline: step 1 sample hardware-aware circuits; step 2 filter circuits by KTA; step 3 compute the training-free proxy ensemble; step 4 rank aggregation and choice of top-k; step 5 evolution by layer augmentation and randomized gate pruning, looping back to step 2. papers.what_it_is: A training-free, evolutionary quantum architecture search for quantum feature maps, ranked by proxy metrics and tested with QSVM on simulators and IBMQ devices. Every one of the 17 pages was read, the reference list included.

existing.note: The Conclusion states this. The paper reports no RBF kernel result in any table or figure, so "particularly RBF-based ones" is the authors' statement without a measurement in this paper.

Confirmed as the Abstract states it. The Experiments section also lists classical datasets (binary MNIST, FMNIST, Breast Cancer) beside the quantum-native and synthetic ones; see the new assertion on the dataset groups.
Two claims, both confirmed as stated in Limitations and Future Work (proxy reliability; adjacent-qubit restriction). Neither is contradicted elsewhere.

Two claims. (1) Table 4 does not show QuProFS fastest on every dataset: on Coset Elivagar lists 26.1 minutes against QuProFS 36.1. The caption says "consistently achieves the lowest runtime", which Table 4 does not support for Coset. (2) The text says IBMQ circuits "remain on par with the simulator results"; Figure 2 shows real-device bars below the simulator bars on some datasets (see the new from_figure assertion). Table 8 lists 0.80 for two datasets.
existing.value: The authors report that QuProFS offers the fastest runtime among QAS benchmarks while maintaining comparable accuracy, though in Table 4 the listed runtime for Elivagar on Coset (26.1) is lower than that for QuProFS (36.1). They also report that QuProFS circuits run on IBMQ devices maintain competitive accuracy, with Table 8 listing 0.80 for H. Manifold and L. Separable.
existing.anchor: Conclusion, p.7; Table 4, p.7; Table 8, p.14
quotes: Our results show that this method offers the fastest runtime among QAS benchmarks while maintaining comparable accuracy.
Despite the presence of noise and decoherence, QuProFS circuits maintain competitive accuracy, demonstrating robustness and practical viability on real quantum hardware

assertions.value: The authors propose an evolutionary training-free quantum architecture search framework that uses circuit-based heuristics for trainability, hardware robustness, generalisation ability, expressivity, complexity and kernel-target alignment.
quotes: we propose an evolutionary training-free quantum architecture search (QAS) framework that employs circuit-based heuristics focused on trainability, hardware robustness, generalisation ability, expressivity, complexity, and kernel-target alignment.
assertions.certainty_reason: The Abstract states what the paper proposes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the search space is sampled from three categories of circuits: hardware-efficient-ansatz-style circuits, covariant feature maps and noise-aware unstructured circuits.
quotes: We further promote diversity by sampling circuits from three distinct categories:
Covariant Feature Maps
Noise-aware Unstructured Circuits

assertions.value: The authors state that all candidate circuits use the hardware native gate set and that two-qubit gates act only on adjacent qubits according to the device connectivity.
quotes: all candidate circuits are composed using the hardware’s native gate set, with two-qubit gates restricted to act only on adjacent qubits according to the device’s connectivity constraints.

assertions.value: The authors state that candidates with the lowest KTA scores are discarded early and that the experiments filter out 80% of the circuits at this step.
assertions.anchor: Circuit Filtering, p.4; Search Procedure, p.6
quotes: Candidates with the lowest KTA scores (bottom p%) are discarded early
For the KTA filtering step, we filter out 80% of the circuits.

assertions.value: The authors state that the ranking uses an ensemble of training-free proxies: a Kernel Concentration Indicator, a Local Effective Dimension for trainability and an Expressivity measure given by the KL divergence to the Haar distribution.
quotes: Kernel Concentration Indicator.
Local Effective Dimension. In order to assess the trainability of each circuit, we estimate their effective dimension using a Monte Carlo approximation of the Fisher Information Matrix
We compute the KL divergence between the circuit’s output state distribution and the Haar distribution to assess expressivity

assertions.value: The authors define the Kernel Concentration Indicator as the Frobenius norm between the fidelity kernel and the matrix of all ones, and state that it indicates how far the kernel is from uniformity.
assertions.anchor: Appendix, Proxies, Degree of Uniformity, p.15
quotes: where the frobenius norm is calculated between the fidelity kernel F of size n × n and the matrix of all ones 1 of size n × n.
This score also gives an indication of how far the kernel is from uniformity.

assertions.value: The authors state that a lower Expr value (KL divergence from the Haar distribution) indicates that a parameterized circuit produces a broader variety of states, and that they favor circuits in the middle range of expressibility because highly expressive circuits are prone to overfitting.
quotes: Lower Expr value indicates that a PQC can produce a broader variety of states within Hilbert space, reflecting enhanced expressibility.
since highly expressive circuits are prone to overfitting, we emphasize selecting circuits that are ranked in the middle range of expressibility.

assertions.value: The authors state that they consider only the local effective dimension because it shows positive correlation with global effective dimension while requiring less time to compute.
quotes: we consider only local effective dimension as it shows positive correlation with global effective dimension while requiring lesser time to compute.
assertions.certainty_reason: No evidence for the correlation is given in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the rank aggregation is a hybrid: proxies in one group are best-ranked prioritized and proxies in the other group are mid-ranked prioritized, preferring circuits that avoid extremes such as excessive depth or expressivity, and that KTA is excluded from the final aggregation.
quotes: Let the proxies in M1 be the best-ranked prioritized, favoring circuits optimal under these criteria and
Proxies in M2 are mid-ranked prioritized, preferring circuits that avoid extremes such as excessive depth or expressivity.
We exclude KTA from this final aggregation since it serves as an initial filter to remove poorly aligned circuits

assertions.value: The authors hypothesize that proxies like dataset compatibility may reflect performance in simulation, while hardware robustness, trainability and expressivity are more relevant to real-device behavior.
quotes: We hypothesize that while proxies like dataset compatibility may reflect performance in simulation, others such as hardware robustness, trainability, and expressivity are more relevant to real-device behavior.
assertions.certainty_reason: A stated hypothesis; the paper does not test it separately.

assertions.value: The authors state that the evolution uses two operations: layer augmentation (exploitation, appending a new layer sampled from the original distribution) and randomized gate pruning (exploration, random gate removal at a tunable rate).
quotes: we introduce two key operations: (a) layer augmentation and (b) randomized gate pruning.
In each refinement cycle, a subset of circuits undergoes random gate removal at a tunable rate

assertions.value: The authors state that in each refinement cycle they randomly select approximately 50% of circuits and apply gate pruning with a probability of 40%, a tunable rate.
quotes: We randomly select approximately 50% of the circuits from the current pool in each refinement cycle.
we apply gate pruning with a probability of 40%, meaning roughly 40% of the gates are removed.

assertions.value: The paper states Theorem 1: for datasets of size N with parameter dimension d, under bounded circuit depth and width and assuming exploitable low-rank structure with a Nystrom subsample size much smaller than N, QuProFS returns near-optimal architecture proxies with high probability, with a per-iteration runtime bound in terms of the proxy accuracy delta, Fisher parameters, expressibility samples and tolerance-dependent exponents alpha and beta.
quotes: Theorem 1 (Runtime guarantee for QuProFS). For datasets of size N with parameter dimension d, under bounded
assuming exploitable lowrank structure with Nystro¨m subsample size M ≪ N , QuProFS returns near-optimal architecture proxies with high probability.
where δ controls proxy accuracy, κ and µ are Fisher matrix parameters, S is expressibility samples, and α, β > 0 depend on approximation tolerances.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement is quoted, but the paper gives only a cost breakdown, not a proof of "near-optimal architecture proxies"; the exponents are left unspecified.
assertions.reader_inference: The result bounds runtime; it does not bound the quality of the selected circuits, although the statement says near-optimal proxies.

assertions.value: The authors state that the per-iteration runtime is dominated by proxy evaluation, that the fidelity proxy still incurs a quadratic cost in the subsample size, and that the evolutionary step is lightweight.
quotes: Theorem 1 shows that the runtime of QuProFS is dominated by proxy evaluation
though the fidelity proxy still incurs a quadratic cost in M
In contrast, the evolutionary step is lightweight, involving simple gate edits with minimal overhead.
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived from the paper's own cost model, not measured.

assertions.value: The authors state that they model the single forward pass time cost as order n D and the gradient with the parameter-shift rule as order n D times the number of variational parameters.
quotes: The single forward pass time cost is modeled as O(nD), for the gradient with parameter shift, we model with O(nDΘ)
assertions.reader_inference: The main-text per-iteration bound and the Appendix per-iteration bound use different cost models and different parameters.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Nystrom low-rank approximation with subsample size much smaller than N reduces the quadratic kernel complexity from order N squared to order N times M squared.
quotes: reduces the quadratic kernel complexity from O(N 2) to O(N M 2)
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated in the appendix cost analysis.

assertions.value: The authors state that hardware robustness is scored with relative fidelity from gate errors, readout error and CNOT count, with a consistent layout, which avoids the expensive layout optimization.
quotes: Our noise-aware cost function incorporates gate and readout errors, as well as CNOT count, enabling reliable comparison across circuits with a consistent layout.
This avoids the expensive task of layout optimization, which involves subgraph isomorphism over large device connectivity graphs.

assertions.value: The authors state that the formula used in the mapomatic score does not cover the entire noise model of the circuit, though it helps assess relative performance of circuits for a given layout.
quotes: While the formula employed in the mapomatic score does not cover the entire noise model of the quantum circuit, it helps assess the relative performance for a set of circuits given the layout.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the limit of its own noise proxy.

assertions.value: The authors state that they evaluate binary classification tasks in three groups: classical (binary MNIST, FMNIST, Breast Cancer), quantum-native (Coset-10) and synthetic (Linearly Separable, Hyperplane Parity, Two Curves, Hidden Manifold).
quotes: We evaluate QuProFS across a diverse suite of binary classification tasks, categorized into three groups:
Quantum-native: Group-structured datasets such as Coset-10, based on hidden subgroup structure

assertions.value: The authors state that features are standardized, reduced by PCA to the input size, datasets are split 80/20 into training and testing, and real-device tests use 8 representative datasets.
quotes: We standardize features and apply dimensionality reduction using PCA
Datasets are split 80/20 for training/testing.
Realdevice tests are conducted on 8 representative datasets using selected circuits.

assertions.value: The authors state that the evolutionary search runs for up to 3 iterations per dataset.
quotes: Our evolutionary architecture search is run for up to 3 iterations per dataset.
assertions.reader_inference: The runtime experiment states two search iterations (three metric evaluations and two evolution rounds); the two statements describe different settings or are inconsistent.

assertions.value: The authors state that they benchmark against publicly available implementations of QuantumSEA, QuantumNAS and Elivagar.
quotes: We benchmark QuProFS against publicly available implementations of leading QAS methods, including QuantumSEA

assertions.value: The authors state that the runtime experiment uses 150 circuits per iteration for two search iterations, the full dataset (all under 1500 samples) for kernel estimation and a subsample of 60 circuits for the local effective dimension.
quotes: We set 150 circuits per iteration for two search iterations (three metric evaluations and two evolution rounds).
For kernel estimation, we use the full dataset (all < 1500 samples), while for LED, we subsample to 60 circuits to manage gradient costs

assertions.value: The authors state that circuits were run on IBM Quantum devices chosen by availability and connectivity, with the top-ranked architectures evaluated on 8 representative datasets.
quotes: We deploy quantum circuits on real quantum hardware from IBM Quantum, including
Due to hardware constraints, we evaluate the top-ranked architectures on 8 representative datasets.

assertions.value: The authors report that QuProFS reaches 0.99 accuracy on Two Curves, and 0.99 and 0.97 on MNIST-2 and FMNIST-2, and state that it surpasses all baselines on those classical benchmarks.
quotes: achieving 0.99 accuracy on Two Curves.
QuProFS reaches 0.99 and 0.97 respectively, surpassing all baselines.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 6 lists qSVM baselines at 0.99 on MNIST-2 and 0.99 on FMNIST-2, equal to or above QuProFS, so "all baselines" holds only against the QAS methods.

assertions.value: The authors report in Table 7 that on Two curves QuProFS reaches 0.99 +/- 0.01 against 0.80 for QSEA, 0.87 for QNAS and 0.73 for Elivagar.
quotes: Two curves Acc.

assertions.value: The authors report in Table 7 that on Hidden manifold QuProFS reaches 0.89 +/- 0.01 while QNAS reaches 0.93, and that on Linearly separable QuProFS, QSEA and QNAS reach 0.93.
assertions.reader_inference: QNAS (gradient-based) is above QuProFS on Hidden manifold and ties it on Linearly separable, so QuProFS does not lead on every synthetic dataset, against the text claim that it "outperforms all QAS and training-free baselines".

assertions.value: The authors report in Table 7 that on Bars and Stripes QuProFS reaches 0.92 +/- 0.01 (QSEA 0.78, QNAS 0.86, Elivagar 0.83) and on Hyperplane 0.96 +/- 0.01 (QSEA 0.87, QNAS 0.80, Elivagar 0.86).

The authors report in Table 7 that the fixed qSVM baselines reach 1.00 on Two curves, and the optimized ZZ qSVM baseline reaches 1.00 on Linearly separable and 0.99 on Hidden manifold, above the QuProFS values.
assertions.reader_inference: The qSVM baselines with standard feature maps match or beat QuProFS on several synthetic datasets, so the search does not beat a fixed feature map there.

assertions.value: The authors report in Table 6 that on Coset-10 QuProFS reaches 0.86 +/- 0.01 against 0.87 for Elivagar, and on Breastcancer 0.92 +/- 0.02 against 0.63 for Elivagar.
quotes: QSEA QNAS Elivagar QuPROFS(Ours)
assertions.reader_inference: Table 3 on p.5 lists Breast Cancer for QuProFS as 0.89, Table 6 lists 0.92 +/- 0.02; the paper does not reconcile them.

papers.title_in_file: Guided sampling ansätzes for variational quantum computing
sections_read: II. Results: A. Guided sampling ansatz

figures.shows: Schematic of the map Psi from the parameter space Theta (left blob, point theta) to the state representation space F (large disc): the ansatz covers a subset of F containing |Psi(theta)>, the optimized state |Psi*>, the guiding state |Psi0> and the ground state |Psi_g>, with the deviation delta Psi* between |Psi*> and |Psi_g>.
figures.confirmed_by: the GSA is constructed using measurements of the guiding state

figures.shows: (a) CVQE workflow: on the QPU, guiding state preparation then sampling; on the CPU, trial state construction from the samples then optimization to E* = minimum over theta of the energy expectation. (b) Circuit component for one Pauli tensor product term: Ry and Rx basis rotations, a CNOT ladder, a central Rz(c_r t) rotation, then the inverse ladder and rotations.
figures.confirmed_by: The implementation of a GSA.

figures.shows: Energy in Ha (y, about -75.5 to -73.0) against O-H bond length in Angstrom (x, 0.5 to 2). Three series: exact ground state (line), guiding state (blue dots, from the IonQ Aria samples) and optimized state (dark red dots). The optimized state lies on the ground state curve (minimum about -75.4 Ha near 1.0 A); the guiding state lies above it (about -74.8 Ha near 1.0 A, about -73.1 Ha at 0.5 A).
figures.confirmed_by: The guiding states |Ψ0⟩ and their energies were calculated classically for K = 1, ε = 0.11 Ha, and T = 2ℏ.

figures.shows: Energy error in Ha (left y, 0 to 0.002) and state deviation norm square (right y, 0 to about 5e-4) against T in inverse Ha (x, -2 to 2) for H3O+ at bond length 1.0 A. papers.what_it_is: A superconducting-qubit VQE experiment on H2, LiH and F2 (up to 12 qubits) with an optimised UCC ansatz, grouped measurement and four error-mitigation methods, with supplementary calibration, method and noise-analysis detail. Every one of the 40 pages was read, the reference list included.

existing.note: Confirmed as the Abstract states it. The 12-qubit molecule (F2) did not reach chemical accuracy; chemical accuracy was reached for H2 (4 qubits) and LiH (6 qubits) at small bond distances, with the LiH average over all plotted distances given as 1.802 mHa in Table I (p.38) and 0.815 mHa when distances above 2.6 Angstrom are excluded (p.5).

Three limits. (1) The headline factor of about two orders of magnitude is the raw error against REM+CF+CMX in Table I (p.38). (2) Symmetry verification is not part of that stack: the SI says SV combined with Clifford fitting gives large fluctuation and that SV results for LiH and F2 were not shown (p.37); Table I has no SV entry for F2, and SV with CF is worse than CF alone for H2 and LiH. (3) "12 selected qubits" holds only for F2; H2 uses 4 qubits and LiH uses 6.
existing.value: The authors report, on the 66-qubit superconducting processor Zuchongzhi 2.0 using up to 12 selected qubits, that error mitigation with readout error mitigation, Clifford fitting and connected moment expansion lowers the average absolute energy error from 143.661 mHa to 0.565 mHa for H2, from 233.564 mHa to 1.802 mHa for LiH and from 1.8315 Ha to 0.0174 Ha for F2 (Table I), which they describe as a gain of around two orders of magnitude; they state that symmetry verification combined with Clifford fitting brought large fluctuation and was not shown for LiH and F2.
